what: Spire distributes natural gas. It is the regulated utility delivering gas to homes and businesses in Missouri, Alabama and Mississippi, operating the pipelines and meters, and it also owns gas storage and midstream assets.
customers: Households and businesses in Missouri, Alabama and Mississippi heating with natural gas, with rates set by each state’s regulator.
money: Regulated gas distribution across three states, principally St. Louis and Alabama.
Storage, pipeline and gas marketing operations.
moat: A regulated gas distribution utility is a legal monopoly in its territory with rates set to allow a return on invested capital. Nobody else may deliver gas to those customers, the network cannot be duplicated, and replacing ageing cast-iron pipe earns a regulated return — which makes earnings growth predictable when regulators cooperate.
risks: Debt of $3.9B against $5.7M of cash is very heavy relative to a $5.1B market value, and it makes the company highly sensitive to interest rates.
Free cash flow was about negative $363.8M, because the utility is investing heavily in pipe replacement.
The shares trade at about 32.7 times earnings and 14.9 times EV/EBITDA, which is expensive even for a regulated utility.
Missouri’s regulatory environment has at times been less generous than peers, and rate case outcomes have disappointed.
Long-term electrification of heating reduces gas demand, which is a structural question for every gas distributor.
opportunities: A regulated monopoly across three states produces predictable, inflation-adjusted revenue.
Last year’s net margin was 19.4%, strong for a gas distributor.
Pipe replacement programmes earn a regulated return on the capital spent, which grows earnings reliably.
St. Louis and Alabama have large installed customer bases with old infrastructure that must be replaced.
Ten analysts average a $91.60 target, about 7% above the current price.
watch: Rate base growth and rate case outcomes. A regulated utility earns the allowed return on invested capital, so those two things determine almost all of the earnings.
view: Spire is a conventional regulated gas distributor, and the mechanics of that are worth restating because they explain the whole investment. The regulator allows the company to earn a return on the capital it has invested in its pipes and meters. Replacing ageing cast-iron pipe in St. Louis is therefore not a cost to be minimised but the engine of earnings growth — spend the money, add it to the rate base, earn the allowed return on it. Spire has a great deal of old pipe, which is an asset in this framework.

The negative free cash flow of $364 million is that programme running, not a problem. But the $3.9 billion of debt against a $5.1 billion market value is a genuine issue, because a utility this leveraged is extremely sensitive to interest rates. The allowed return is set in rate cases that happen every few years, while the cost of new debt moves continuously, so a period of rising rates squeezes the utility until the next case catches up.

The regulatory jurisdiction matters more than most investors weigh. Missouri has at times been among the less generous regulators, and rate case outcomes there have disappointed. A utility’s earnings are entirely a function of what the regulator allows, so the same pipe replacement programme produces different results in different states — and this is not something management can fix.

At 32.7 times earnings and 14.9 times EV/EBITDA, Spire is priced above most gas distributors, which is hard to justify given the leverage and the regulatory record. Ten analysts seeing 7% of upside suggests the market agrees it is fully valued. The long-dated headwind is heating electrification, which is slow and politically contested in these states but points one way. Rate base growth and rate case outcomes are the only numbers that matter, and the revenue line — which swings with gas prices passing through — should be ignored entirely.
bull: A large old network keeps feeding rate base growth at allowed returns in states with stable customer bases, producing dependable earnings and a reliable dividend.
bear: Rates stay high against $3.9 billion of debt while Missouri regulators deny full recovery, and a 33 times earnings multiple on a utility derates.
